transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I suppose... well, my daughter, she’s the one who made the appointment, but I suppose what brings me in is that I just don’t have the push I used to have. It’s hard to explain, really. I used to be so involved in things, you know? I’ve been singing in the church choir for going on thirty years, and I used to look forward to Tuesday night rehearsals like you wouldn't believe. We’d sing, and then Mary—she’s the alto next to me—would always bring these little lemon squares she makes. But lately, I just... I can't seem to get myself out the door for it. And it's not just choir. I used to quilt with a group of ladies on Thursdays. We were working on a beautiful double wedding ring pattern for my niece, but I haven't been in weeks. I don't even have the energy to go visiting folks like I used to. I know people are expecting me, I know they're probably wondering where I am, but most days, I just sit at home in my armchair. I don't even really watch anything, I just leave the TV on low, just for the noise, I suppose. It’s just... everything feels like such an effort now, and I just sit there thinking about all the things I should be doing, but I just can't seem to make myself do them.
How long have you been feeling this way—this lack of energy and difficulty doing things you used to enjoy?

Well, let me think back on that, Doctor. It hasn't been just a sudden thing, like catching a cold where you wake up one morning and you're sick. It’s been more of a... a slow creep, I suppose you could say. It really started building up right around the time I retired from the school office. That was a little over two years ago now. 

I used to help out down at the elementary school, just doing bits and pieces in the front office, answering the phones, making sure the little ones got their lunch boxes if they left them on the bus, things like that. I loved seeing the children every day. And they had a beautiful little send-off for me when I finished up, they really did, with a big sheet cake from the grocery store and a nice card signed by all the teachers. 

At first, you know, right after that, I thought I was just enjoying the rest. I thought, well, I’ve earned a bit of time in my armchair, not having to rush out the door at half-past six in the morning in the freezing cold. I thought it was just a little vacation for my bones. But then... well, the weeks turned into months, and now it's been those two years and a bit, and that resting just sort of turned into this... this heavy feeling. I just never got my momentum back after I left the school. I told my daughter I was going to take up more hobbies with all that free time, maybe do more of my quilting, but instead, it's just been these past two years of slowly doing less and less, until now where I just... I can't even get myself down to the church.
Have you noticed any changes in your memory, or do you find yourself having trouble with things you used to do automatically, like cooking or managing your finances?

Well, my memory... I suppose it's about the same as it's always been, really. I mean, I might forget where I put my reading glasses now and then, but that's just because I set them down when I'm looking at the mail and then I wander off to the kitchen. But as far as the cooking goes... well, I just don't do it much anymore. It's not that I've forgotten how. I used to make a pot roast every Sunday, with the carrots and the little red potatoes, cooked slow all afternoon until it just fell apart on your fork. My husband, Lord rest him, he used to say nobody made a roast like mine. And my gravy! I always made it from scratch, none of those little packets for me. But now... well, getting all those ingredients out, chopping the vegetables, standing over the stove... it just seems like a mountain to climb. I just can't bring myself to do it. So I'll just have a piece of toast, or maybe heat up a can of soup if I'm feeling up to turning on the burner. 

And the finances, well, my daughter helps me with that mostly. Not because I can't add up the numbers—I worked in the school office, you know, I was always good with the petty cash box. But she just started coming over on the first of the month and sitting at the kitchen table with me to go through the bills. She'll open the envelopes and say, "Okay, Mom, here's the electric bill," and I'll write the check. I know how to write a check, of course I do. But if she wasn't there... I don't know, the envelopes might just sit in that little brass holder on the counter for a while. It's not that I don't understand them, it's just... the thought of opening them all up and getting out the stamps and the return address labels... it just feels so heavy. So, no, I don't think I've forgotten how to do these things, I just... I just don't have the steam to do them anymore.

Over these past two years, have you noticed that you're having trouble remembering things that happened recently—like conversations you had last week, or appointments you need to keep—things that you would normally remember easily?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I don't think so. It's like I said before, I might misplace my reading glasses or maybe I'll forget why I walked into the kitchen—you know how that is, you get up from your chair with a purpose, and by the time you cross the threshold, the thought has just vanished right out of your head! But as far as real conversations or appointments... no, I remember those just fine. 

Like last Tuesday, my neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, called. She lives in the blue house two doors down, the one with the lovely hydrangea bushes out front. She called to tell me about her grandson's graduation, and we talked for a good twenty minutes about how quickly time passes. I remember every word of it. She was telling me he's going off to study engineering, which is so impressive, don't you think? And she was worried about him being so far away in another state. I can recall all of that clear as a bell. 

And my appointments, well, I remember them, even if I don't always have the energy to go. I knew I had my dental cleaning last month. Dr. Evans, he’s been my dentist for fifteen years, such a gentle man. I had it written right there on the calendar in the kitchen, the one with the Thomas Kinkade paintings that my daughter gets me every Christmas. I knew it was coming up for weeks. I saw it there, I remembered it, but when the day actually came, I just... I couldn't get myself dressed and out the door. I had to call his receptionist, Susan—lovely girl, always asks after my daughter—and cancel. 

So it's not the remembering that's the problem, Doctor. The memory is still there, ticking away like a clock on the mantel. It's just the doing that I can't seem to manage anymore. I remember what I'm supposed to do, I just sit there and think about it instead of doing it.

Over these past two years, would you say that most days you feel sad or down in your mood, or do you feel more of an emptiness or numbness? Or is it mainly just this lack of energy and motivation without necessarily feeling sad?

Well, you know, it’s a funny thing you ask that, because my daughter and I were just talking about this... or well, she was talking and I was listening. I wouldn't call it sad, exactly. It’s not like when my husband passed away, Lord rest his soul, where you feel that terrible heavy ache in your chest and you just want to cry all day. It’s not like that at all. I don't sit around weeping or feeling sorry for myself. It’s more just... well, what brings me in is I just don’t have the push I used to have. 

I used to be so busy, always on the go. Like with the church choir—I’ve sung alto in that choir for going on twenty years, and we practice every Thursday evening. I never missed a Thursday. But now, I just can't seem to get my coat on to go. And my quilting, too. I have this lovely Double Wedding Ring pattern I started, all the little pieces cut out from old dresses and shirts, just sitting right there in my sewing basket next to my chair. But I just look at it. I don't have the drive to even thread the needle. I don't even go visiting folks anymore, not even Mrs. Higgins down the street, and I used to always bring her a slice of my banana bread when I baked. 

Now, most days, I just sit at home in my armchair. I'll have the television on, but just on low, you know, just a little murmur in the background so the house doesn't feel too quiet. Maybe a game show or the local news, just flickering away while I sit there. And the thing is, I know people are expecting me. I know Mr. Peterson, our choir director, is looking for me on Thursdays, and the ladies at the church wonder where I am, and my daughter expects me to be doing my sewing. I know they're waiting on me. But I just sit there with the TV on low anyway. So no, I wouldn't say I'm heartbroken or sad, it's just... the get-up-and-go has completely got up and left, and there's just a sort of blankness where my energy used to be.

Do you find yourself worrying a lot about things—either things that might happen in the future, or things going on right now? And if so, is it hard for you to stop those worries once they get started?

Worrying? No, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier. Not anymore, anyway. You know, my daughter, she is the one who worries enough for the whole family now. She will come over and ask if I am worried about the electric bill going up, or if I heard about the weather reports getting bad. And I just look at her. I mean, I remember a time when I would have fussed over every little thing. When my husband was still working down at the plant, I used to pace the floor if there was a snowstorm, worrying about the roads being slick, making sure I had a hot thermos of coffee ready for him the minute he walked through the door. I used to fret about whether the Sunday roast was too dry or if the church ladies thought my dress was out of season. 

But now... well, like I was saying before with the television and the sitting, it is like I just don't have the energy to worry. Worrying takes a lot of effort, doesn't it? You have to sit there and spin it around and around in your head, thinking about what if this happens and what if that happens. And my head just... it just doesn't spin like that anymore. It is too quiet for all that noise. So when things happen, or when the news is on and they are talking about the economy or whatever trouble is going on in the world, it just washes right over me. I don't get tied up in knots about tomorrow. Tomorrow is just going to be another day of me sitting in my armchair with the TV on low, so there isn't much to fret over, is there? It is just empty of all that fussing. So no, I don't find myself worrying about much of anything at all.

Before these past two years when you started feeling this way, have there been other times in your life—maybe months or even years apart—when you felt this same kind of heaviness and lack of energy, where things that used to bring you joy just didn't anymore?

Well... no. No, I really don't think so. It's like I was just saying, this... this sitting around, this blankness, it's all new. Just these past two years, really. 

You see, I’ve worked hard my whole entire life. I actually had to leave school back in the eighth grade—my mother needed help at home with the little ones, there were six of us in that tiny house, you know, and somebody had to wash the cloth diapers and tend the stove and keep the younger ones out of the road. So I’ve always been doing *something*. I never had the luxury of just losing my energy or letting things go. 

Even when times were truly hard... like when the mill closed down for a spell back in the seventies and my husband was out of work and we didn't know how we'd pay for the groceries. Or like I mentioned before, when he passed away. That was a terrible time, just terrible. We had been married forty-two years, and the house felt so big and empty without him. But even then, even with all that grief and the crying, I didn't lose my drive like this. I still got up every single morning, put on my face, made sure the house was presentable. I kept things spotless. You could eat right off my kitchen linoleum, I scrubbed it so well every Tuesday morning with the ammonia and hot water. I still went to choir, I still baked. 

So no, I’ve never had a time like this before. Never in my life. It’s just these last couple of years where the battery just completely ran out, like a toy that just stops walking. Before this, I was always on the move. Always. If I wasn't quilting, I was baking, and if I wasn't baking, I was out weeding the tomatoes in the backyard. I used to grow the biggest beefsteak tomatoes on the block, Mrs. Higgins used to say so herself every August when I'd bring her a basket. But no... never any time before now where I just stopped caring about doing those things. This is the very first time my get-up-and-go just decided not to come back.

I want to make sure I understand your history correctly. You mentioned you've never felt this way before these past two years. But I'm wondering—have you ever had a period, even a shorter one, maybe weeks or a month or two, where you felt down or depressed or lost interest in things, even if it wasn't quite as long or as severe as what you're experiencing now?

No, doctor, not even for a week or two. I know you want to be thorough and make sure you've got it all down right, but it's just exactly like I said. I never had anything like this happen before, not even for a short spell. 

I mean, even when things were truly exhausting... oh, I remember back in, I think it was '88 or maybe '89? My sister, Margaret, she came down with a terrible case of pneumonia. She was in the county hospital for nearly a month, and I was the one going back and forth every single day. I had to take two different buses just to get out there, and the second bus was always running late, especially in the winter. And I'd sit by her bed, fluffing her pillows and making sure the nurses were bringing her fresh water, and then I'd ride those two buses all the way back home in the dark. 

But even then, with all that going on and me being tired down to my bones, I never lost my interest in my life. I'd walk through the front door, take off my boots, and I'd still get my sewing out, or I'd start a nice meatloaf for supper. I never had a time where I just sat and stared at the wall. It just wasn't in my nature at all. My mother, Lord rest her, she used to say I was like a little wind-up toy that didn't know how to wind down. She’d say, "You better sit down before you wear out my good floorboards." 

So no, not a month, not a week, not even a couple of days. If I was awake, I was doing something. I was keeping the house, or I was helping at the church bake sales. We used to do these big spring sales to raise money for the new choir robes, and I was always, always in charge of the pie table. Dozens of pies, doctor. Cherry, apple, rhubarb when it was in season... I'd be up until two in the morning rolling out crusts on my kitchen counter, getting flour all over my apron. And I loved doing it. I never, not once, had a time where I looked at my rolling pin and thought, "I just don't care," or felt too heavy to pick it up. That just never happened to me. Not until these last two years. It's really just like somebody found a switch on my back and turned it off, and the power just hasn't come back on since. So no, nothing like this before, short or long.

patient.answer:
Well, you know, it’s a funny thing you ask that, because my daughter and I were just talking about this... or well, she was talking and I was listening. I wouldn't call it sad, exactly. It’s not like when my husband passed away, Lord rest his soul, where you feel that terrible heavy ache in your chest and you just want to cry all day. It’s not like that at all. I don't sit around weeping or feeling sorry for myself. It’s more just... well, what brings me in is I just don’t have the push I used to have. 

I used to be so busy, always on the go. Like with the church choir—I’ve sung alto in that choir for going on twenty years, and we practice every Thursday evening. I never missed a Thursday. But now, I just can't seem to get my coat on to go. And my quilting, too. I have this lovely Double Wedding Ring pattern I started, all the little pieces cut out from old dresses and shirts, just sitting right there in my sewing basket next to my chair. But I just look at it. I don't have the drive to even thread the needle. I don't even go visiting folks anymore, not even Mrs. Higgins down the street, and I used to always bring her a slice of my banana bread when I baked. 

Now, most days, I just sit at home in my armchair. I'll have the television on, but just on low, you know, just a little murmur in the background so the house doesn't feel too quiet. Maybe a game show or the local news, just flickering away while I sit there. And the thing is, I know people are expecting me. I know Mr. Peterson, our choir director, is looking for me on Thursdays, and the ladies at the church wonder where I am, and my daughter expects me to be doing my sewing. I know they're waiting on me. But I just sit there with the TV on low anyway. So no, I wouldn't say I'm heartbroken or sad, it's just... the get-up-and-go has completely got up and left, and there's just a sort of blankness where my energy used to be.

doctor.intent: Differentiate between major depressive disorder (F32.9/F33.9) and generalized anxiety disorder (F48.0) by assessing whether the patient experiences persistent worry or anxious thoughts that are difficult to control, which would be central to GAD but less typical of depression.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself worrying a lot about things—either things that might happen in the future, or things going on right now? And if so, is it hard for you to stop those worries once they get started?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of anxiety and excessive worrying, which are not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Worrying? No, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier. Not anymore, anyway. You know, my daughter, she is the one who worries enough for the whole family now. She will come over and ask if I am worried about the electric bill going up, or if I heard about the weather reports getting bad. And I just look at her. I mean, I remember a time when I would have fussed over every little thing. When my husband was still working down at the plant, I used to pace the floor if there was a snowstorm, worrying about the roads being slick, making sure I had a hot thermos of coffee ready for him the minute he walked through the door. I used to fret about whether the Sunday roast was too dry or if the church ladies thought my dress was out of season. 

But now... well, like I was saying before with the television and the sitting, it is like I just don't have the energy to worry. Worrying takes a lot of effort, doesn't it? You have to sit there and spin it around and around in your head, thinking about what if this happens and what if that happens. And my head just... it just doesn't spin like that anymore. It is too quiet for all that noise. So when things happen, or when the news is on and they are talking about the economy or whatever trouble is going on in the world, it just washes right over me. I don't get tied up in knots about tomorrow. Tomorrow is just going to be another day of me sitting in my armchair with the TV on low, so there isn't much to fret over, is there? It is just empty of all that fussing. So no, I don't find myself worrying about much of anything at all.

inference.note: Ruled out F48.0 (Neurasthenia). Patient denies significant worry and anxiety, which would be expected in neurasthenia. The presentation is consistent with Major Depressive Disorder - anhedonia (loss of interest in choir, quilting, visiting), anergia (lack of energy/push), apathy (can't get herself to do things despite remembering them), and lack of sadness (depression without prominent mood symptoms). Two-year duration with gradual onset after retirement. Cannot yet distinguish between single episode (F32.9) vs. recurrent (F33.9) without history of prior episodes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced previous episodes of depression that have remitted, which would distinguish recurrent depression (F33.9) from a single major depressive episode (F32.9)
doctor.question: Before these past two years when you started feeling this way, have there been other times in your life—maybe months or even years apart—when you felt this same kind of heaviness and lack of energy, where things that used to bring you joy just didn't anymore?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of previous depressive episodes or periods of low energy and anhedonia prior to the current onset, which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well... no. No, I really don't think so. It's like I was just saying, this... this sitting around, this blankness, it's all new. Just these past two years, really. 

You see, I’ve worked hard my whole entire life. I actually had to leave school back in the eighth grade—my mother needed help at home with the little ones, there were six of us in that tiny house, you know, and somebody had to wash the cloth diapers and tend the stove and keep the younger ones out of the road. So I’ve always been doing *something*. I never had the luxury of just losing my energy or letting things go. 

Even when times were truly hard... like when the mill closed down for a spell back in the seventies and my husband was out of work and we didn't know how we'd pay for the groceries. Or like I mentioned before, when he passed away. That was a terrible time, just terrible. We had been married forty-two years, and the house felt so big and empty without him. But even then, even with all that grief and the crying, I didn't lose my drive like this. I still got up every single morning, put on my face, made sure the house was presentable. I kept things spotless. You could eat right off my kitchen linoleum, I scrubbed it so well every Tuesday morning with the ammonia and hot water. I still went to choir, I still baked. 

So no, I’ve never had a time like this before. Never in my life. It’s just these last couple of years where the battery just completely ran out, like a toy that just stops walking. Before this, I was always on the move. Always. If I wasn't quilting, I was baking, and if I wasn't baking, I was out weeding the tomatoes in the backyard. I used to grow the biggest beefsteak tomatoes on the block, Mrs. Higgins used to say so herself every August when I'd bring her a basket. But no... never any time before now where I just stopped caring about doing those things. This is the very first time my get-up-and-go just decided not to come back.

doctor.intent: Determine if this is a single depressive episode (F32.9) versus recurrent depressive disorder (F33.9) by clarifying whether there have been any previous episodes of depression, even if milder or differently expressed than the current presentation
doctor.question: I want to make sure I understand your history correctly. You mentioned you've never felt this way before these past two years. But I'm wondering—have you ever had a period, even a shorter one, maybe weeks or a month or two, where you felt down or depressed or lost interest in things, even if it wasn't quite as long or as severe as what you're experiencing now?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of shorter depressive episodes (feeling down or losing interest) prior to the current 2-year period. My symptom profile does not contain an item for past depressive episodes.

patient.answer:
No, doctor, not even for a week or two. I know you want to be thorough and make sure you've got it all down right, but it's just exactly like I said. I never had anything like this happen before, not even for a short spell. 

I mean, even when things were truly exhausting... oh, I remember back in, I think it was '88 or maybe '89? My sister, Margaret, she came down with a terrible case of pneumonia. She was in the county hospital for nearly a month, and I was the one going back and forth every single day. I had to take two different buses just to get out there, and the second bus was always running late, especially in the winter. And I'd sit by her bed, fluffing her pillows and making sure the nurses were bringing her fresh water, and then I'd ride those two buses all the way back home in the dark. 

But even then, with all that going on and me being tired down to my bones, I never lost my interest in my life. I'd walk through the front door, take off my boots, and I'd still get my sewing out, or I'd start a nice meatloaf for supper. I never had a time where I just sat and stared at the wall. It just wasn't in my nature at all. My mother, Lord rest her, she used to say I was like a little wind-up toy that didn't know how to wind down. She’d say, "You better sit down before you wear out my good floorboards." 

So no, not a month, not a week, not even a couple of days. If I was awake, I was doing something. I was keeping the house, or I was helping at the church bake sales. We used to do these big spring sales to raise money for the new choir robes, and I was always, always in charge of the pie table. Dozens of pies, doctor. Cherry, apple, rhubarb when it was in season... I'd be up until two in the morning rolling out crusts on my kitchen counter, getting flour all over my apron. And I loved doing it. I never, not once, had a time where I looked at my rolling pin and thought, "I just don't care," or felt too heavy to pick it up. That just never happened to me. Not until these last two years. It's really just like somebody found a switch on my back and turned it off, and the power just hasn't come back on since. So no, nothing like this before, short or long.

inference.note: Ruled out F33.9 (recurrent depressive disorder). Patient explicitly denies any previous episodes of depression, low mood, or loss of interest in activities throughout her entire life before these past 2 years. This is a single depressive episode with insidious onset following retirement, not a recurrent pattern. The presentation is consistent with F32.9 (major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified).

Meets DSM-5/ICD-10 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, chronic.
